questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Which peoples are Australia's first inhabitants?
options: Convicts who arrived from Great Britain
Free settlers from Great Britain and Ireland
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
questions.explanation: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples were the first people to live in Australia, long before European settlement.
questions.sourceSection: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Which statement about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples is correct?
options: They have the oldest continuous cultures and traditions in the world
They arrived in Australia with the First Fleet
They came to Australia during the gold rush
questions.explanation: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures and traditions are the oldest continuous ones in the world.
questions.sourceSection: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: According to the archaeological record, when did Aboriginal peoples arrive in Australia?
questions.explanation: Archaeological evidence shows that Aboriginal peoples arrived in Australia between 65,000 and 40,000 years ago.
questions.sourceSection: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Where are Torres Strait Islander people from?
options: Islands in Bass Strait, between Victoria and Tasmania
Islands between the northern tip of Queensland and Papua New Guinea
Islands off the west coast of Western Australia
questions.explanation: Torres Strait Islander people come from the islands that lie between Queensland's northern tip and Papua New Guinea.
questions.sourceSection: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: How many convict ships were in the First Fleet?
questions.explanation: The First Fleet was the first group of 11 convict ships to arrive from Great Britain.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: When did the First Fleet arrive from Great Britain?
questions.explanation: The First Fleet arrived on 26 January 1788, which marked the start of European settlement.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Why did the British Government send convicts to the new colony of New South Wales?
options: Convicts were needed to fight in World War I
British jails could not hold the large number of prisoners
Gold had been found in New South Wales
questions.explanation: British laws were harsh at the time and the jails were overcrowded, so convicts were transported to New South Wales.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Who was the first Governor of the colony of New South Wales?
questions.explanation: Captain Arthur Phillip was the first Governor of the colony of New South Wales.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Where did the early free settlers come from?
questions.explanation: Early free settlers came from Great Britain and Ireland, and this heritage has strongly shaped Australia's history, culture and politics.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: In which year did a gold rush begin in New South Wales and Victoria?
questions.explanation: A gold rush began in 1851 when gold was discovered in the colonies of New South Wales and Victoria.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: During the gold rush, which people became the first large group of migrants from outside Europe?
questions.explanation: Chinese people who arrived during the gold rush were the first large group of migrants who were not from Europe.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: What happened to Australia's population in the 10 years after the gold rush began?
questions.explanation: The gold rush drew people from around the world, and within 10 years the population more than doubled.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: What was formed when the separate colonies united in 1901?
options: The colony of New South Wales
The Australian and New Zealand Army Corps
questions.explanation: In 1901 the separate colonies joined together in a federation of states called the Commonwealth of Australia.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: After which event were Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples included in official estimates of the Australian population?
questions.explanation: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples were left out of official population estimates until after the 1967 Referendum.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Which group came to Australia in large numbers after World War II?
options: Convicts transported from the jails of Great Britain
Gold miners who came from China to look for gold
People from Europe who had to leave their homelands
questions.explanation: After World War II a wave of non-British migration arrived, as millions of people in Europe had to leave their homelands.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: How many distinct Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages are there?
questions.explanation: There are more than 100 distinct Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages, and they are valued in Australia.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: How many states and mainland territories does Australia have?
options: Six states and two mainland territories
Seven states and one mainland territory
Five states and three mainland territories
questions.explanation: Australia is a federation of six states and two mainland territories.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Which city is Australia's national capital?
questions.explanation: Canberra is Australia's capital city, and each state and mainland territory also has its own capital.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: What is the capital city of Western Australia?
questions.explanation: Perth is the capital of Western Australia, the largest state.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Brisbane is the capital city of which state?
questions.explanation: Brisbane is the capital of Queensland, Australia's second largest state.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Which was the first colony established by the British in Australia?
questions.explanation: New South Wales was the first colony the British established, and its capital, Sydney, is now the nation's largest city.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Which is Australia's largest state?
questions.explanation: Western Australia is the largest state, and Queensland is the second largest.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Which is Australia's smallest state?
questions.explanation: Tasmania is the smallest state, while Victoria is the smallest of the mainland states.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: What separates Tasmania from the mainland?
questions.explanation: Tasmania is an island state, separated from the mainland by Bass Strait.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: The Great Barrier Reef runs along the coast of which state?
questions.explanation: The world-famous Great Barrier Reef runs along Queensland's eastern coast.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Uluru, Kata Tjuta and Kings Canyon are icons of which part of Australia?
questions.explanation: Uluru, Kata Tjuta and Kings Canyon are icons of the Northern Territory, whose capital is Darwin.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Cradle Mountain, Port Arthur and the Bay of Fires are icons of which state?
questions.explanation: Cradle Mountain, Port Arthur and the Bay of Fires are all Tasmanian icons.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Where are Parliament House and the High Court of Australia located?
options: Sydney, in the state of New South Wales
Canberra, in the Australian Capital Territory
questions.explanation: The Australian Capital Territory lies between Sydney and Melbourne and contains Canberra, home to national institutions such as Parliament House and the High Court.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Who performs a Welcome to Country?
options: The most senior politician or official at the event
An Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander custodian of the local region
Any guest at the event, whatever their background
questions.explanation: A Welcome to Country is performed by a local Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander custodian to welcome visitors to their traditional land.
questions.sourceSection: Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Who can deliver an Acknowledgement of Country?
options: Only an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander Elder
questions.explanation: Anyone can give an Acknowledgement of Country to show respect for the Traditional Custodians of the land.
questions.sourceSection: Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: On which date is Australia Day celebrated each year?
questions.explanation: Australia Day is celebrated on 26 January and is a public holiday in every state and territory.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: What anniversary does Australia Day mark?
options: The arrival of the First Fleet from Great Britain in 1788
The joining of the colonies into one nation in 1901
The landing of Australian troops at Gallipoli in 1915
questions.explanation: Australia Day is the anniversary of the First Fleet's arrival from Great Britain in 1788.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Who announces the Australian of the Year Awards during Australia Day celebrations?
options: The Premier of New South Wales
questions.explanation: During Australia Day celebrations, the Prime Minister announces the Australian of the Year Awards in Canberra.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: On which date is Anzac Day commemorated each year?
questions.explanation: Anzac Day is commemorated on 25 April, the anniversary of the 1915 landing at Gallipoli.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Where did the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps land on 25 April 1915?
questions.explanation: Anzac Day is named after the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps, which landed at Gallipoli in Türkiye during World War I.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Who do Australians remember on Anzac Day?
options: The convicts and sailors who arrived on the First Fleet in 1788
All Australians who served and died in wars, conflicts and peacekeeping operations
The leaders who joined the colonies together to form one nation
questions.explanation: Anzac Day is a solemn day to remember the sacrifice of Australians who served and died in wars, conflicts and peacekeeping operations.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: What are the colours of the Australian National Flag?
questions.explanation: The Australian National Flag is blue, white and red.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: How many points does the Commonwealth Star on the Australian National Flag have?
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth Star has seven points: one for each of the six states and one for the territories.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: What does the Union Jack on the Australian National Flag represent?
options: The six states and the territories
The stars seen in the southern sky
questions.explanation: The Union Jack in the top left corner represents Australia's history of British settlement and the laws and institutions inherited from it.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Which flag is black, red and yellow?
questions.explanation: The Australian Aboriginal Flag is black, red and yellow.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: On the Australian Aboriginal Flag, what does the yellow circle represent?
questions.explanation: The yellow circle stands for the sun; the black top half represents Aboriginal peoples and the red bottom half represents the earth.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: On the Torres Strait Islander Flag, what does the blue panel in the centre represent?
questions.explanation: The blue panel represents the sea, while the green stripes represent the land.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: On the Torres Strait Islander Flag, what is the symbol for all Torres Strait Islanders?
questions.explanation: The white dancer's headdress in the centre of the flag is a symbol for all Torres Strait Islanders.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Which animals support the shield on the Commonwealth Coat of Arms?
questions.explanation: A kangaroo and an emu, both native Australian animals, hold up the shield, one on each side.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: What does the Commonwealth Coat of Arms identify?
options: The authority and property of the Commonwealth of Australia
The members and leaders of the largest political party
The capital cities of each of the states and territories
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth Coat of Arms is the official symbol of the Commonwealth and identifies its authority and property.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: What does the shield on the Commonwealth Coat of Arms represent?
options: The ships of the First Fleet
questions.explanation: The shield in the centre of the Coat of Arms represents the six states and federation.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: What is Australia's national flower?
questions.explanation: The golden wattle is Australia's national flower, and it also forms the background of the Coat of Arms.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: In which season does the golden wattle have its golden yellow flowers?
questions.explanation: The golden wattle is a small tree with bright green leaves and many golden yellow flowers in spring.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: What are Australia's national colours?
questions.explanation: Green and gold are the national colours because they are the colours of the golden wattle.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: What is Australia's national gemstone?
questions.explanation: The opal is the national gemstone; an Aboriginal legend says a rainbow touching the earth created its colours.

questions.partTitle: Australia and its people
questions.question: Which song is Australia's national anthem?
questions.explanation: 'Advance Australia Fair' is the national anthem, sung at events such as citizenship ceremonies and major sporting events.

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: What is Australia's system of government?
questions.explanation: Australia's system of government is a parliamentary democracy, where the people vote for representatives in parliament.

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: In Australia's parliamentary democracy, where does the power of government come from?
questions.explanation: The power of government comes from the Australian people, who vote for their representatives in parliament.

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: How do representatives in parliament answer to the people for their decisions?
questions.explanation: Representatives in parliament must answer to the people, through elections, for the decisions they make.

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: What does the Rule of Law mean?
options: All Australians are equal under the law
Laws apply only to Australian citizens
Leaders can decide which laws to follow
questions.explanation: Under the Rule of Law, all Australians are equal under the law and no one is above it.

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: Who must obey Australia's laws?
options: Everyone, including leaders and the police
questions.explanation: No person, group or religious rule is above the law, and this includes government, community and religious leaders, business people and the police.

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: According to Australia's democratic beliefs, how should change happen?
options: Through discussion, peaceful persuasion and the democratic process
Through violence if other ways are too slow
Through the decisions of religious leaders
questions.explanation: Australians believe change should come through discussion, peaceful persuasion and the democratic process, and they reject violence.

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: How are Australians expected to treat each other, whatever their background?
questions.explanation: All Australians are expected to treat each other with dignity and respect, regardless of things like race, gender, religion or wealth.
questions.sourceSection: Respect for all individuals regardless of background

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: Which freedom allows people to say and write what they think?
questions.explanation: Freedom of speech means people can say and write what they think and discuss their ideas with others.
questions.sourceSection: Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: As long as they obey the law, what can people in Australia do under freedom of speech?
options: Damage property to protest against the government
Threaten people who disagree with them
Criticise the government and protest peacefully
questions.explanation: People can criticise the government, protest peacefully and campaign to change laws, as long as they obey Australian laws.
questions.sourceSection: Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: Which freedom covers expressing views through art, film, music and literature?
questions.explanation: Freedom of expression means people can express their views, including through art, film, music and literature.
questions.sourceSection: Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: What is freedom of association?
options: The right to follow any religion you choose
The right to form and join groups to pursue common goals
The right to vote in a secret ballot
questions.explanation: Freedom of association is the right to form and join associations, such as a political party or trade union, to pursue common goals.

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: Under freedom of association, can a person be forced to join a group?
options: No, people can choose not to join
Yes, everyone must join a trade union
Yes, voters must join a political party
questions.explanation: People may join any legal organisation, but they can also decide not to join and cannot be forced to.

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: When people gather to protest, what must the gathering be like?
options: Peaceful, with no one hurt and no property damaged
Approved in advance by a religious or community leader
Organised and led by a political party
questions.explanation: Australians can gather to protest, but the gathering must be peaceful, must not injure anyone or damage property, and must obey the law.

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: What religious heritage does Australia have?
questions.explanation: Australia has a Judaeo-Christian heritage and many Australians describe themselves as Christians, while people from all the large religions live here.

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: Which of these is a public holiday because it is a Christian day?
questions.explanation: Australia has public holidays on Christian days such as Good Friday, Easter Sunday and Christmas Day.

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: What does it mean that the government in Australia is secular?
options: It follows the rules of one official religion
It is run by the leaders of the largest church
It operates separately from churches and other religious groups
questions.explanation: A secular government operates separately from churches or other religious entities and treats all citizens equally, whatever their beliefs.

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: Does Australia have an official national religion?
options: Yes, the official religion is Christianity
No, people can follow any religion or none
Yes, each state chooses its own religion
questions.explanation: Australia has no official national religion, and people are free to follow any religion they choose, or none.

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: If an Australian law and a religious practice conflict, which one prevails?
questions.explanation: Religious practices must obey Australian law, and where the two conflict, Australian law prevails.

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: What rights do men and women have in Australia?
options: Men have more rights than women
Rights depend on whether a person is married
questions.explanation: Men and women have equal rights in Australia, and it is against the law to discriminate against someone because of their gender.

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: What does Australia's value of a 'fair go' aim to ensure?
options: That wealthy families get the best jobs
That there are no formal class distinctions
That older people always come first
questions.explanation: A 'fair go' means equal opportunity, where success comes from talent, work and effort rather than wealth or background.
questions.sourceSection: Equality of opportunity and a 'fair go'

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: Which of these is a responsibility of Australian citizenship?
options: Serving on a jury if called to do so
questions.explanation: The responsibilities of citizenship are to obey the law, vote, defend Australia should the need arise, and serve on a jury if called.

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: Which of these is a privilege of Australian citizenship?
options: Serving on a jury if called
questions.explanation: Applying for an Australian passport and re-entering Australia freely is a privilege, while obeying the law and jury service are responsibilities.

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: Which of these is listed as both a responsibility and a privilege of Australian citizenship?
options: Serving on a jury if called
questions.explanation: Voting in federal and state or territory elections, and in a referendum, appears in both lists.
questions.sourceSection: Responsibilities and privileges of Australian citizenship

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: At what age do Australian citizens have a responsibility to vote?
questions.explanation: Voting is a responsibility, right and privilege for Australian citizens aged 18 years or over.
questions.sourceSection: Voting in federal and state or territory elections, and in a referendum

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: What is a referendum?
options: A vote to choose the Prime Minister
A vote to change the Australian Constitution
A vote to elect local councillors
questions.explanation: A referendum is a vote on changing the Australian Constitution, and citizens aged 18 or over have a responsibility to vote in it.
questions.sourceSection: Voting in federal and state or territory elections, and in a referendum

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: In which elections is voting compulsory?
options: Federal and state or territory elections
questions.explanation: Voting is compulsory in federal and state or territory elections.
questions.sourceSection: Voting in federal and state or territory elections, and in a referendum

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: In some states, voting may be optional in which elections?
questions.explanation: In some states it may not be compulsory to vote in local government elections, unlike federal and state or territory elections.
questions.sourceSection: Voting in federal and state or territory elections, and in a referendum

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: Is service in the Australian Defence Force compulsory?
options: Yes, for all men aged 18 to 25
questions.explanation: Service in the Australian Defence Force is voluntary, but citizens have a responsibility to defend Australia should the need arise.
questions.sourceSection: Defend Australia should the need arise

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: What does a jury do?
options: Makes new laws for the parliament
Hears the evidence and decides if a person is guilty
Chooses which judge hears a case
questions.explanation: A jury is a group of ordinary Australians who listen to the evidence in a court case and decide whether a person is guilty or not guilty.
questions.sourceSection: Serve on a jury if called to do so

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: Which Australian citizens can be called to serve on a jury?
options: Citizens who are on the electoral roll
Only citizens who work for the government
questions.explanation: Citizens on the electoral roll can be called for jury service, which is a responsibility for citizens aged 18 or over.
questions.sourceSection: Serve on a jury if called to do so

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: What does jury service help to ensure?
options: That parliament can pass laws faster
That the court system is open and fair
That the police decide who is guilty
questions.explanation: When ordinary citizens serve on juries, it helps keep the court system open and fair.
questions.sourceSection: Serve on a jury if called to do so

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: Which of these is a job in the Australian Public Service?
options: Working at the Australian Taxation Office
questions.explanation: Citizens can apply to work for the Australian Government in the Australian Public Service, for example at Services Australia or the ATO.
questions.sourceSection: Apply for work in the Australian Public Service and the Australian Defence Force

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: What does the Australian Defence Force include?
options: The Army, Navy and Air Force
questions.explanation: The Australian Defence Force is made up of the Army, Navy and Air Force, and citizens can apply to work in it.
questions.sourceSection: Apply for work in the Australian Public Service and the Australian Defence Force

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: Which Australian citizens can seek election to parliament?
options: Those aged 18 or over who are not dual citizens
Only citizens who were born in Australia
questions.explanation: Citizens aged 18 or over who do not hold dual citizenship can stand for election to federal, state or territory parliament.

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: When an Australian citizen returns from overseas, do they need a visa to re-enter Australia?
options: No, citizens can return without a visa
Yes, they need a tourist visa
Yes, unless they travelled for work
questions.explanation: Australian citizens have the right to live freely in Australia and can return from overseas without needing a visa.
questions.sourceSection: Apply for an Australian passport and re-enter Australia freely

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: While overseas, whose laws must Australian citizens obey?
options: Only the laws they agree with
The laws of the country they are in
questions.explanation: Australian citizens overseas can ask Australian officials for help, but they must obey the laws of the country they are in.
questions.sourceSection: Ask for consular assistance from an Australian official while overseas

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: How can Australian officials help citizens who are overseas in an emergency?
options: By paying any fines they receive
By excusing them from local laws
questions.explanation: Australian officials at embassies, high commissions and consulates can help in emergencies, for example by issuing an emergency passport.
questions.sourceSection: Ask for consular assistance from an Australian official while overseas

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: If an Australian citizen has a child born overseas, what can they apply for?
options: For the child to become a citizen by descent
For the child to be exempt from Australian law
For the child to vote before turning 18
questions.explanation: One privilege of citizenship is applying for a child born overseas to become an Australian citizen by descent.
questions.sourceSection: Apply for children born overseas to become Australian citizens by descent

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: Who collects tax in Australia?
questions.explanation: Paying tax is required by law, and tax on money earned from a job, business or investments is collected by the ATO.

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: What are taxes spent on?
options: Services such as healthcare, education and defence
questions.explanation: Taxes pay for services including government-funded healthcare and education, defence, roads and railways, and social security.

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: Why is freedom of speech important in Australia?
options: It allows people to make false claims about others
It lets people ignore laws they dislike
questions.explanation: Freedom of speech is a core Australian value that underpins the democratic system, but Australian laws must still be obeyed.
questions.sourceSection: Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

questions.partTitle: Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.question: Why do our representatives in government make laws?
options: To keep society orderly, free and safe and protect rights
To protect the interests of wealthy people
To give political parties more power
questions.explanation: Representatives make laws to maintain an orderly, free and safe society and to protect people's rights, and everyone in Australia must obey them.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What must Australian citizens aged 18 or over do before they can vote?
options: Pass a test on the Constitution
questions.explanation: Citizens aged 18 or over must enrol to vote, and people who are not correctly enrolled cannot vote in an election.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Which organisation conducts federal elections and referendums?
questions.explanation: The AEC runs federal elections and referendums and maintains the Commonwealth electoral roll.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Which statement about the Australian Electoral Commission is correct?
options: It is run by the largest political party
It is independent of the government
It is controlled by the Prime Minister
questions.explanation: The AEC is independent, and political parties or people in government cannot influence its decisions.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What does it mean that voting in Australia is by secret ballot?
options: Your vote is read out at the polling place
Your employer is told how you voted
You vote in private and are free to choose any candidate
questions.explanation: Because voting is by secret ballot, you are free and safe to vote for any candidate you choose.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What may happen if you fail to vote in an election without a good reason?
options: You may have to pay a fine
You will lose your Australian citizenship
You will be banned from voting in future elections
questions.explanation: Voting is compulsory, so failing to vote without a good reason may result in a fine.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: How can citizens raise concerns about government policy?
options: By asking a judge to change the policy
By asking the police to change the policy
questions.explanation: Citizens can contact their elected representative about government policy, and the representative should consider their suggestions.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Before 1901, how was Australia organised?
options: As six separate, self-governing British colonies
As one British colony run from Sydney
questions.explanation: After British settlement and before 1901, Australia was made up of six separate British colonies, each with its own constitution and laws.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Which problem did the separate colonies have before federation?
options: Trade and transport between them was expensive and slow
They had no laws or constitutions of their own
They were all governed by one shared parliament
questions.explanation: Before federation, trade and transport between colonies was slow and costly, enforcing laws across borders was hard, and defence was weak.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: On what date did the Australian Constitution come into effect?
questions.explanation: The Constitution came into effect on 1 January 1901, when the colonies became one nation, the Commonwealth of Australia.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What is the Australian Constitution?
options: A list of Australia's national symbols
The pledge new citizens make at their ceremony
The legal document setting out the basic rules of government
questions.explanation: The Constitution is the legal document that sets out the basic rules for how Australia is governed.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: How was the Australian Constitution originally passed?
options: By a vote of all Australians in the 1967 Referendum
As part of a British Act of Parliament in 1900
By a decision of the High Court of Australia in 1901
questions.explanation: The Constitution was first passed as part of a British Act of Parliament in 1900, and it came into effect in 1901.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Which two Houses make up the Parliament of the Commonwealth of Australia?
options: The House of Representatives and the Cabinet
The House of Representatives and the Senate
The Senate and the High Court
questions.explanation: The Constitution set up the Australian Parliament with two Houses: the House of Representatives and the Senate.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Which body has the ultimate power to apply and interpret the laws of Australia?
questions.explanation: The Constitution also set up the High Court, which has the final say in applying and interpreting Australia's laws.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Who can change the Australian Constitution?
options: The Australian people, by voting in a referendum
The Prime Minister and Cabinet, by a Cabinet vote
The Governor-General, by signing an order
questions.explanation: The Constitution can be changed when the Australian people vote for the change in a referendum.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: In the 1967 Referendum, what share of Australians voted 'Yes'?
questions.explanation: More than 90 per cent of Australians voted 'Yes' in the 1967 Referendum.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What change did the 1967 Referendum allow?
options: The colonies to join together as one nation
Aboriginal peoples to be counted in the Census
questions.explanation: The 1967 Referendum changed the Constitution so that Aboriginal peoples could be counted in the Census.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What is needed for a referendum to change the Australian Constitution?
options: The approval of the Governor-General only
A majority of voters in any one state
questions.explanation: A double majority means a majority of voters across the nation and a majority of voters in a majority of states must vote for the change.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Why does the Constitution divide the power of government into three branches?
options: To allow laws to be made more quickly
To give the King a day-to-day role in government
To stop one person or group from holding all the power
questions.explanation: Power is split between the legislative, executive and judicial branches so that no single person or group holds all of it.
questions.sourceSection: How is the power of government controlled?

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What is legislative power?
options: The power to make and change laws
The power to put laws into practice
The power to interpret and apply laws
questions.explanation: Legislative power belongs to Parliament, whose members are elected by the people.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What is the power to put laws into practice called?
questions.explanation: Executive power puts laws into practice; the Executive includes the Prime Minister, government ministers and the Governor-General.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Who has the power to interpret and apply the law?
questions.explanation: Judicial power belongs to judges, and courts and judges are independent of parliament and government.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Who is Australia's Head of State?
questions.explanation: The King of Australia is the Head of State, and the Governor-General is his representative in Australia.
questions.sourceSection: Who is Australia's Head of State?

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Who appoints the Governor-General?
options: The King, on the advice of the Prime Minister
The voters, at a federal election
The Senate, by a vote of its members
questions.explanation: The King of Australia appoints the Governor-General as his representative, acting on advice from the Prime Minister.
questions.sourceSection: Who is Australia's Head of State?

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What does it mean that Australia is a constitutional monarchy?
options: The King runs the government day to day
The Prime Minister is also the Head of State
The King is Head of State but must act in line with the Constitution
questions.explanation: In a constitutional monarchy the King is Head of State, but he must act in accordance with the Constitution.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Which statement about the Governor-General is correct?
options: The Governor-General leads the largest political party
The Governor-General is elected by the Senate
questions.explanation: The Governor-General is not part of the government, acts independently of all political parties and must stay neutral.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What is it called when the Governor-General signs a Bill passed by Parliament into law?
questions.explanation: Signing Bills passed by Parliament into law is called Royal Assent and is one of the Governor-General's roles.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Who is the Commander-in-Chief of the Australian Defence Force?
questions.explanation: Acting as Commander-in-Chief of the Australian Defence Force is one of the Governor-General's roles.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Which of these is a role of the Governor-General?
options: Starting the process for a federal election
questions.explanation: The Governor-General's roles include starting the process for a federal election, performing ceremonial duties and giving Royal Assent.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What is the title of the leader of a state government?
questions.explanation: A state government is led by the Premier, while a territory government is led by the Chief Minister.
questions.sourceSection: Who are some of Australia's leaders?

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What is the title of the leader of a territory government?
questions.explanation: The leader of a territory government is the Chief Minister.
questions.sourceSection: Who are some of Australia's leaders?

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Who represents the King in each Australian state?
questions.explanation: Each state has a Governor who represents the King, in a role similar to the Governor-General's.
questions.sourceSection: Who are some of Australia's leaders?

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Who is the leader of a local government?
questions.explanation: A local government is led by a Mayor or Shire President, and councillors are the elected members of the council.
questions.sourceSection: Who are some of Australia's leaders?

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What is the Australian Government also called?
options: The State Government or the Local Council
The Federal Government or the Commonwealth Government
The Crown Government or the Royal Government
questions.explanation: The Australian Government is also known as the Federal Government or the Commonwealth Government.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What is another name for the House of Representatives?
questions.explanation: The House of Representatives is also known as the Lower House or the People's House; the States' House and the House of Review are names for the Senate.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Who does each member of the House of Representatives represent?
options: Only the members of their political party
A whole state, with every state equally represented
The people in their federal electorate
questions.explanation: Australia is divided into federal electorates, and each member of the House of Representatives represents the people in their electorate.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: How is the number of House of Representatives members for each state and territory decided?
options: By the number of people living there
Every state and territory has the same number
By the land area of the state or territory
questions.explanation: The number of MPs for each state and territory is based on how many people live there.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Which House of Parliament is also called the States' House?
questions.explanation: The Senate is sometimes called the Upper House, the House of Review or the States' House.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: How many senators are there in total?
questions.explanation: There are 76 senators in total: 12 from each state and two from each of the two mainland territories.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: How many senators does each state elect?
questions.explanation: Each state elects 12 senators, so all states are equally represented regardless of size or population.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: How many senators do the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory each elect?
questions.explanation: The Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory elect two senators each.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Who appoints the Administrator of the Northern Territory?
options: The voters of the Northern Territory
questions.explanation: The Administrator of the Northern Territory is appointed by the Governor-General and has a role similar to that of a state Governor.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: How do the states differ from the territories?
options: States have rights recognised by the Constitution; territories do not
Territories have their own constitutions; states do not
Only territories can pass their own laws
questions.explanation: States have constitutional rights and can pass laws in their own right, while the Australian Government can change or revoke self-governing territory laws.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What do the Australian states each have?
options: Their own separate Head of State
questions.explanation: Each state government has its own parliament and constitution, and works in a similar way to the Australian Government.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Which level of government is responsible for rubbish collection?
questions.explanation: Local governments are responsible for services such as rubbish collection, local roads, parks and libraries.
questions.sourceSection: What do the three levels of government do?

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Which level of government is mainly responsible for hospitals and schools?
questions.explanation: State and territory governments are primarily responsible for hospitals and health services, schools, police and public transport.
questions.sourceSection: What do the three levels of government do?

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Which level of government is responsible for immigration and citizenship?
questions.explanation: The Australian Government handles immigration and citizenship, along with defence, foreign affairs, taxation and social security.
questions.sourceSection: What do the three levels of government do?

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Which of these is a responsibility of the Australian Government?
questions.explanation: Defence is an Australian Government responsibility, while rubbish collection is handled by local government and public transport by state and territory governments.
questions.sourceSection: What do the three levels of government do?

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Which level of government is responsible for building permits?
questions.explanation: Local governments look after building permits, as well as parks, drains and local libraries.
questions.sourceSection: What do the three levels of government do?

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What is a political party?
options: A group of people who share ideas about how a country should be governed
A court of law that hears cases about disputed elections
A government department that collects tax from voters
questions.explanation: A political party is a group of people with similar ideas about how the country should be governed; the main parties include the Liberal Party, Labor, the Nationals and the Greens.
questions.sourceSection: What role do political parties play in the way Australia is governed?

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What are members of parliament without a political party called?
questions.explanation: Most members of parliament belong to a political party; those who do not are called independents.
questions.sourceSection: What role do political parties play in the way Australia is governed?

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: After a federal election, who generally forms the Australian Government?
options: The party with the most members in the Senate
The party or coalition with a majority in the House of Representatives
The party with the most members in state parliaments
questions.explanation: The government is generally formed by the party or coalition with a majority in the House of Representatives, and its leader becomes Prime Minister.
questions.sourceSection: How is the Australian Government formed?

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What is the party or coalition with the second largest number of members in the House of Representatives called?
questions.explanation: The party or coalition with the second largest number of members forms the Opposition, led by the Leader of the Opposition.
questions.sourceSection: How is the Australian Government formed?

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What is the Cabinet?
options: The key decision-making body of government
The lower house of a state parliament
The group that conducts federal elections
questions.explanation: The Cabinet is made up of the ministers with the most important portfolios and is the government's key decision-making body.
questions.sourceSection: How is the Australian Government formed?

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Who approves the appointment of the Prime Minister and ministers?
questions.explanation: The Prime Minister recommends who should be ministers, and the Governor-General approves the appointment of the Prime Minister and ministers.
questions.sourceSection: How is the Australian Government formed?

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What is a proposal for a new law, or a change to an existing law, called?
questions.explanation: A proposed new law or change to a law is called a Bill, and both Houses of Parliament debate and vote on it.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What happens to a Bill after a majority in each House of Parliament agrees to it?
options: It goes to a referendum of all voters
It goes to the High Court for approval
It goes to the Governor-General to be signed into law
questions.explanation: Once both Houses pass a Bill, it goes to the Governor-General, who signs it into law.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What does a court decide in a criminal case?
options: Which political party forms the government
Whether a person has broken the law and, if so, the penalty
Who should be elected to the Senate
questions.explanation: Australian courts are independent and decide whether a person has broken the law and what the penalty is, based only on the evidence.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What can courts base their decisions on?
options: What the police tell them to decide
questions.explanation: Courts can only base their decisions on the evidence put before them.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Can the government remove a judge because it disagrees with the judge's decisions?
options: Yes, the Prime Minister can remove any judge
questions.explanation: Judges and magistrates are appointed by the government, but the government cannot take away their jobs because it disagrees with their decisions.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: In Australia, how is a person treated until they are found guilty in a court?
options: As a suspect who has no rights
questions.explanation: In Australia, people are considered innocent until a court finds them guilty, and everyone can be represented by a lawyer.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: In a criminal trial, who decides the penalty if the jury finds a person guilty?
questions.explanation: The judge explains the law to the jury, and if the jury finds a person guilty, the judge decides the penalty.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: How do the police relate to the government in Australia?
options: The police take their orders from the Prime Minister
The police are run by the largest political party
The police are independent of the government
questions.explanation: Police maintain peace and order and are independent of the government, but it is the court that decides guilt.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What is the name of Australia's national police force?
questions.explanation: The Australian Federal Police is the national police force; it investigates crimes against federal laws.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: What does the Australian Federal Police investigate?
options: Crimes against federal laws, such as drug trafficking
Breaches of local council building permits
Tax returns that are lodged late
questions.explanation: The AFP investigates crimes against federal laws, such as drug trafficking and crimes against national security or the environment.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Is it legal to offer a bribe to a police officer in Australia?
options: Yes, if the amount of money is small
No, even offering a bribe is a crime
Yes, for minor offences such as parking
questions.explanation: Bribing police is a serious crime in Australia, and even offering a bribe to a police officer is a crime.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: A person breaks a law they were unaware of. Can they use this as an excuse?
options: No, not knowing the law is no excuse
Yes, if they are new to Australia
Yes, if it is their first offence
questions.explanation: Everyone must become familiar with Australian laws, because not knowing the law is no excuse for breaking it.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Which statement about domestic and family violence is correct?
options: It is a private family matter and not a crime
It is allowed if it happens inside the home
questions.explanation: Domestic and family violence, such as hitting or controlling a partner through fear, is against the law, and a person who commits it can go to jail.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Who controls road and traffic rules in Australia?
questions.explanation: Road and traffic rules are controlled by state and territory governments, and breaking them can lead to a fine or prison.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Who must wear a seatbelt when travelling in a car in Australia?
options: Only passengers in the front seat
questions.explanation: Everybody travelling in a car must wear a seatbelt, and babies and young children must be in an approved car seat.

questions.partTitle: Government and the law in Australia
questions.question: Which of these is against the law while driving in Australia?
questions.explanation: Traffic laws are strict: it is illegal to use a hand-held mobile device while driving, or to drive after taking drugs or above the blood alcohol limit.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Which ideas are Australian values based on?
options: Wealth, social class and family background
Loyalty to one religion and one political party
Freedom, respect, fairness and equality of opportunity
questions.explanation: Australian values are based on freedom, respect, fairness and equality of opportunity, and they help keep Australia secure, prosperous and peaceful.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: What are all Australians expected to do with Australian values?
options: Follow them only when it suits them
Replace them with the values of their home country
questions.explanation: Australian values are shared by everyone, and all Australians are expected to respect, share and uphold them.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: When should you follow Australian laws?
options: Only when the police can see you
At all times, even when no one is watching
Only when the law agrees with your culture
questions.explanation: Everybody should obey the law at all times, and you should follow it even if no one is watching.
questions.sourceSection: Commitment to the Rule of Law

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Do Australian laws apply to people of every background and culture?
options: No, migrants can follow the laws of their home country
No, only people born in Australia must follow them
Yes, everyone in Australia must follow Australian laws
questions.explanation: Whatever your background or culture, you must follow Australian laws, and no person or group is above the law.
questions.sourceSection: Commitment to the Rule of Law

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: What happens to people who break the law in Australia?
options: Nothing, if they did not know about the law
Nothing, if they are community leaders
questions.explanation: Everybody should obey the law and not break it at any time, otherwise they will face penalties.
questions.sourceSection: Commitment to the Rule of Law

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: In Australia, who determines the laws?
questions.explanation: In Australia's parliamentary democracy, laws are determined by parliaments elected by the people, so citizens are involved in how the country is governed.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Under freedom of speech, how freely can people in Australia express their ideas?
options: Without any limits, even if it breaks the law
Only with permission from the government
Freely, as long as it is within the law
questions.explanation: People in Australia can express their ideas freely and say or write what they think, but they must stay within the law.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Which statement about newspapers, television and radio in Australia is correct?
options: They must get government approval for every story
They are not allowed to report on protests
They have the same freedom of speech as people
questions.explanation: Newspapers, television and radio outlets have the same freedom of speech that people in Australia have.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Is it acceptable to promote violence against a group because of their religion or culture?
options: No, it is against Australian values and law
Yes, it is part of freedom of speech
Yes, if it is only done online
questions.explanation: It is never acceptable to promote violence against a person or group, for example because of their culture, ethnicity, religion or background.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Which of these is illegal in Australia?
options: Writing to your member of parliament
questions.explanation: Freedom of speech has limits: it is illegal to make false allegations or to encourage others to break the law.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Why is peaceful public protest tolerated in Australia?
options: It gives protesters the right to damage property
It replaces the need for elections
It is an essential part of democracy
questions.explanation: People may protest peacefully against the government, because tolerating peaceful public protest is an essential part of democracy.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Can a person be forced to leave a lawful group they belong to?
options: Yes, if their family wants them to leave
Yes, if their employer wants them to leave
No, people are free to join or leave groups voluntarily
questions.explanation: People are free to join or leave any group voluntarily, as long as it is within the law, and no one can be forced to join an organisation or to leave it.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: What legal status do religious laws have in Australia?
options: The same status as Australian law
They replace Australian law for members of that religion
questions.explanation: Religious laws have no legal status in Australia, and Australian law applies to everyone.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Which statement about polygamy (being married to more than one person at the same time) is correct?
options: It is legal if a person's religion allows it
It is against the law in Australia
It is legal if all the partners agree
questions.explanation: Polygamy is against the law in Australia and can lead to severe legal penalties, including imprisonment.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: What is the legal position of forced marriage in Australia?
options: It is against the law and can lead to imprisonment
It is allowed if both families agree
It is allowed if it is a cultural tradition
questions.explanation: Forced marriage, where one or both people did not freely choose to marry, is illegal and can result in severe penalties, including imprisonment.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: How is religious intolerance viewed in Australian society?
options: It is acceptable towards small religions
It is acceptable if your own religion allows it
questions.explanation: Religious intolerance is not acceptable, and everyone should have an equal opportunity to pursue their goals regardless of their religion.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Under Australian law, how are Buddhists and people of other faiths treated compared with Christians?
questions.explanation: People from different backgrounds are not given preferential treatment; Buddhists and people of all other faiths are treated the same as Christians.
questions.sourceSection: Equality of all people under the law

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Under Australian law, who can marry each other?
options: Only a man and a woman
Two people, including two men or two women
One person and more than one partner at the same time
questions.explanation: Under Australian law two people can marry each other, including two men or two women, but polygamy is illegal.
questions.sourceSection: Equality of all people under the law

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Can women in Australia stand for parliament and join the police?
options: No, only men can do these things
Yes, women and men have equal rights
questions.explanation: Men and women have equal rights, including equal access to education and work, voting, standing for parliament, joining the Defence Force and police, and equal treatment in court.
questions.sourceSection: Equality of all people under the law

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: In Australia, can a woman get a job ahead of a man?
options: No, a man must always be chosen first
Yes, if she has better qualifications and skills
Only if no men apply for the job
questions.explanation: Gender discrimination is against the law, and a woman has the right to get a job ahead of a man if she has better qualifications and skills.
questions.sourceSection: Equality of all people under the law

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Who makes decisions about a person's personal matters, such as marriage and religion?
questions.explanation: Everyone can make their own independent choices about personal matters such as marriage and religion, and the law protects them from intimidation or violence.
questions.sourceSection: Equality of all people under the law

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Which statement about physical violence against a spouse or partner is correct?
options: It is never acceptable and is a criminal offence
It is acceptable if it happens at home
It is a private family matter, not a crime
questions.explanation: Physical violence against a spouse or partner is never acceptable and is a criminal offence in Australia.
questions.sourceSection: Equality of all people under the law

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Who can apply to the courts for a divorce in Australia?
options: Only a couple who both want the divorce
Either a husband or a wife
questions.explanation: Divorce is acceptable in Australia, and either spouse may apply to the courts even if the other wants to stay married.
questions.sourceSection: Equality of all people under the law

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: In Australia, what should a person get a job based on?
questions.explanation: Under a 'fair go', people should get jobs because of their skills and experience, not their gender, wealth or ethnicity.
questions.sourceSection: Equality of opportunity and a 'fair go'

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: What should a person's achievements in life be the result of?
questions.explanation: Australians believe everyone deserves a 'fair go', so what someone achieves should come from their hard work and talents.
questions.sourceSection: Equality of opportunity and a 'fair go'

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: How have many new migrants become leaders in business, the arts, public service and sport?
options: Through wealth they brought with them
questions.explanation: Many new migrants have become leaders in Australia through their hard work and enterprise.
questions.sourceSection: Equality of opportunity and a 'fair go'

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Which statement about verbal and physical abuse is correct?
options: Verbal abuse is legal if it happens at home
questions.explanation: Violence of any kind, including verbal and physical abuse, is illegal in Australia.
questions.sourceSection: Mutual respect and tolerance for others

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: How do Australians believe disagreements should be handled?
options: Peacefully, with everyone free from violence and intimidation
With threats, if the issue is serious enough
With violence, if talking does not work
questions.explanation: Australians believe in peaceful disagreement and, above all, in everyone's right to be safe and free from violence and intimidation.
questions.sourceSection: Mutual respect and tolerance for others

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: What is the age of sexual consent in Australia?
options: 16 or 17, depending on the state or territory
questions.explanation: The age of sexual consent is 16 or 17, depending on which state or territory you live in.
questions.sourceSection: Mutual respect and tolerance for others

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: A 20-year-old man wants to have sexual relations with a 15-year-old girl. Which statement is correct?
options: It is legal if her parents agree
It is illegal in every state and territory
It is legal in some states and territories
questions.explanation: Because the age of consent is 16 or 17, this would be illegal everywhere in Australia.
questions.sourceSection: Mutual respect and tolerance for others

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: What should you do when the police make a lawful request?
options: Obey it only if a lawyer is present
questions.explanation: You should obey a lawful request from the police, because all Australians commit to following the law.
questions.sourceSection: Mutual respect and tolerance for others

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: What does mutual respect mean?
options: Listening to others and respecting their views, even when they differ from yours
Agreeing with everyone in your community to avoid any argument
Respecting only the people who share your own background and beliefs
questions.explanation: Mutual respect means listening to others and respecting their views and opinions, even when they are different from your own.
questions.sourceSection: Mutual respect and tolerance for others

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Racism has no place in Australia. Which of these is an example of racism?
options: Making racially abusive comments at a sporting event
Cheering for a team from another country
questions.explanation: Racism has no place in Australia; examples include racially abusive comments in public or at sporting events, and sharing racially offensive material online.
questions.sourceSection: Mutual respect and tolerance for others

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: What is everyone in Australia expected to try to do when they are able to?
options: Rely on others to support them
Leave all community work to the government
questions.explanation: Everyone is expected to contribute to the community and to try to support themselves and their family when they can.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: What does 'mateship' mean in Australia?
options: Spending time only with people from your own country
Helping each other in times of need
Supporting only the members of your own family
questions.explanation: Australians value mateship, which means helping others, and accepting help, especially in difficult times.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Which of these is an example of compassion for those in need?
options: Only helping people who can pay you back
Staying away from neighbours who are lonely
Driving a friend to a medical appointment
questions.explanation: Showing compassion might mean taking a meal to an elderly neighbour, driving a friend to a medical appointment, or visiting someone who is sick, frail or lonely.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: How strong is Australia's tradition of community service and volunteering?
options: Strong, with many opportunities to volunteer
Weak, because volunteering is not encouraged
Non-existent, because all helpers must be paid
questions.explanation: Australia has a strong tradition of volunteering, which is a great way to share knowledge and learn new skills.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: What role does English play in Australian society?
options: It is the national language and an important unifying element
It is one of several official national languages
It is only needed by people who work for the government
questions.explanation: English is Australia's national language and an important unifying element of society, so people living here should make an effort to learn it.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: If a citizenship applicant's native language is a language other than English, what must they do?
options: Make reasonable efforts to learn English
Pay someone to speak English for them
questions.explanation: Applicants for citizenship must make reasonable efforts to learn English if it is not their native language.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: How does learning English help people living in Australia?
options: It lets them avoid obeying the law
It helps them get an education and a job, and integrate
It lets them vote without enrolling
questions.explanation: English helps people get an education and a job and better integrate into the community.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: What should you do if you suspect a friend or neighbour may be planning a serious crime?
options: Report it to Australian government authorities as soon as possible
Keep it secret to protect your friend or neighbour
Wait until the crime happens and then tell someone
questions.explanation: Everyone has a responsibility to help protect Australian society, which includes reporting a suspected serious crime as soon as possible.
questions.sourceSection: Helping to keep our society safe

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: If you know that a child is being abused, what should you do?
options: Wait until the child asks for help
questions.explanation: Anyone in Australia who sees or knows of a child being abused should report it to the police to investigate.
questions.sourceSection: Helping to keep our society safe

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Which of these is an example of cyber abuse?
options: Sending a birthday message to a friend on social media
Joining an online study group for the citizenship test
Sharing sexual photos of someone online without their consent
questions.explanation: Online abuse is not accepted in Australia, and many forms of cyber abuse, such as sharing sexual images without consent or stalking someone online, are illegal.
questions.sourceSection: Helping to keep our society safe

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: In the citizenship pledge, who do Australian citizens pledge their loyalty to?
options: The political party they vote for
The country where they were born
questions.explanation: In the citizenship pledge, new citizens pledge their loyalty to Australia and its people.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Can an Australian citizen also hold the citizenship of another country?
options: Yes, but only if they were born in Australia
Yes, if the laws of that country allow it
questions.explanation: Australian citizens may also hold the citizenship of another country if that country's laws allow it; this is called dual or multiple citizenship.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: An Australian citizen also holds the citizenship of another country. Which laws must they follow while in Australia?
options: The laws of their other country
All Australian laws, at all times
Only the Australian laws they agree with
questions.explanation: An Australian citizen in Australia must follow all Australian laws at all times, even if they hold another citizenship.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Which law must Australian citizens follow even when they are overseas?
options: The ban on sexual activity with a child under 16
The local council rules on parking and noise
The state rules on public transport tickets
questions.explanation: Some Australian laws apply to citizens overseas; for example, it is illegal to be involved in any sexual activity with a child under 16, in Australia or overseas.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Which of these would undermine Australia's interests and security?
options: Voting for any candidate in a federal election
Using social media to share official government secrets
Volunteering for a local charity or sports club
questions.explanation: Australians share an obligation not to undermine Australia's interests and security, for example by sharing official government secrets on social media.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: What would promoting distrust in and fear of an ethnic community do?
questions.explanation: Promoting distrust in and fear of an ethnic community would damage community relations in Australia.

questions.partTitle: Australian values
questions.question: Under freedom of speech, where can people meet for social or political discussion?
questions.explanation: Freedom of speech means people can meet in public or private to discuss social or political matters, as long as they stay within the law.
